# Always Replace: Understanding Torque-to-Yield Bolts

When you encounter a specification marked "always replace" in a service manual, it is almost exclusively referring to torque-to-yield (TTY) bolts. These are not standard fasteners; they are engineered components designed to undergo significant plastic deformation during installation to achieve their clamping force. The phrase "always replace" is an operational directive born from the physics of how these bolts work, specifically regarding the relationship between yield strength and fatigue life.

In your VW Jetta application, the three bolts securing the suspension ball joint to the lower control arm likely fall into this category. Unlike standard high-tensile bolts that rely solely on friction between threads and under the nut to clamp parts together, TTY bolts are tightened in two distinct stages: an initial snug-to-spec torque (in your case, 20 Nm) followed by a precise angular rotation (90 degrees). This two-step process elongates the bolt shank beyond its elastic limit into the plastic region.

The critical technical detail here is that once a fastener has been stretched past its yield point, it cannot return to its original length. The material microstructure has permanently changed. If you were to remove such a bolt and reinstall it without replacing it, the second torque-to-yield cycle would not be reproducible. The first installation already consumed the bolt's capacity to stretch. Attempting to apply the same 90-degree rotation on a used bolt risks stretching it well beyond its safe operating limit or causing catastrophic failure upon re-torquing.

Furthermore, there is a significant risk of thread galling and damage during removal. TTY bolts are often installed with lubrication, but if they have been torqued to yield, the friction and stress on the threads can cause them to seize in the aluminum control arm. Forcing a used bolt out can strip the threads in the casting, leaving you without a viable mounting point for a new bolt anyway. Therefore, the "always replace" instruction serves as a safety mechanism against thread damage and inconsistent clamping force.

Regarding your concern about alignment shops replacing these bolts: this is highly unlikely to happen unless you explicitly request it or if the shop has access to OEM-grade TTY fasteners in their inventory. Most general alignment facilities operate with standard hex bolts for suspension work because they do not have the specialized tools, such as angle stoppers or digital torque wrenches calibrated for angular tightening, required to properly install TTY bolts. Even if an alignment shop attempts to tighten a bolt, they cannot replicate the specific yield event that occurred during the initial installation.

If you skip replacing these bolts and simply clean and reuse them, you are gambling with the structural integrity of your lower control arm connection. The 90-degree rotation requirement is not arbitrary; it is the specific amount of stretch needed to seat the joint correctly against the mounting surface. Without a fresh bolt, that geometric relationship is compromised.

From a software engineering perspective, this concept mirrors the "single-use token" pattern or disposable cryptographic keys. A token generated for one authentication event contains entropy and state changes that make it invalid for reuse. Similarly, a TTY bolt is single-use by design. Reusing it introduces undefined variables into your systemâvariables like residual stress, thread damage, and altered yield characteristicsâthat can lead to runtime errors, in this case, suspension failure.

While online tutorials often gloss over these specifics to simplify the process for DIYers, relying on those shortcuts with TTY fasteners is a dangerous trade-off. The cost of a few bolts is negligible compared to the repair costs associated with a snapped control arm or catastrophic accident. Always adhere to the "always replace" directive found in manuals like the Bentley service guide to ensure the mechanical integrity of your vehicle remains uncompromised.
